newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania counts on NATO help to restructure army.
newsitem.headline: Albania counts on NATO help to restructure army.

text.p: NATO will help Albania's new Socialist-led government to restructure its armed forces after they fell apart in a popular revolt, Defence Minister Sabit Broka said on Monday.
Thousands of soldiers fled their barracks in March when violence erupted across the country over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes which bankrupted many people in the poor Balkan country.

Even army officers, many of whom stayed at their posts in the early days of the turmoil, returned home for fear of their families' safety when anarchy appeared to be taking over the formerly communist state.

"The restructuring of the Albanian army will be based on a concept worked out with NATO and on agreements with separate nations," Broka said in his first news conference since the coalition government of Prime Minister Fatos Nano came to power last month.

Broka said the aim was to set up a professional body and recruit to the military on three-year paid contracts. The government wanted to employ only as many soldiers as it could afford as regards accommodation and training.
National service of 12 months would be retained.
"(It will be) the necessary number that an army needs to deal with emergencies," said Broka, a Socialist.

Rebuilding of the army seemed to be part of a planned drive to restore law and order in Albania, big swathes of which remain under the thumb of gangsters waging turf wars and terrorising travellers with looted weaponry.

According to figures issued by the International Institute of Strategic Studies for 1995/96, Albania had an army of around 60,000 men, with another 12,500 working in the ill-equipped navy and air force.

A NATO delegation is due in Albania on August 14 to study the current state of the armed forces, whose morale, observers say, has sunk to an all-time low since the communist regime was toppled in 1990.

"The amount of time needed to restructure our armed forces depends on how our country strengthens but especially on the help from NATO and other partners who are very much committed to building our army as soon as possible," Broka said.
Albania was one of the first of Europe's ex-communist states to join NATO's Partnership for Peace programme.
The defence minister said military assistance from NATO and the United States should resume immediately.
It was suspended last year because of major irregularities in general elections. Broka said Tirana had also accepted the deployment of an Italian military mission in Albania.
Italy led a 7,000-strong multinational protection force deployed in Albania in April. The force is due to withdraw fully by mid-August.
The Albanian government is preparing a draft law to be sent to parliament for the collection of weapons, most of which were stolen from army or police depots during the rebellion earlier this year.
Broka said previous assistance to Albania from NATO and other states did not show results because the former Democratic Party government calibrated reforms to suit its own interests.

Accusing the previous government of illegally distributing weapons, Broka said some senior army officers had organised armed units with secret police and had plans to attack some areas in the south where the outbreak of violence was concentrated.
